statements.1:
The Goal

Claim more territory than your opponent across 2 games with colors and first move swapped. The higher combined territory score wins the match.

 Rules

Board and placement

  • Each game starts on an empty 16 by 16 board.
  • Blue plays first. Blue and Orange then alternate, placing 1 stone per turn.
  • A placement must be on an empty cell with no stone in any of its 8 neighboring cells, including diagonals. This applies to stones of either color.
  • Neighbors outside the board are ignored. On an empty board, every cell is legal.
  • Stones never move or disappear. Passing is not allowed.

Cell coordinates and action indices

Rows are numbered from 0 at the top to 15 at the bottom. Columns are numbered from 0 on the left to 15 on the right.

Every cell has an integer action index. Start at 0 in the top-left corner, count from left to right, then continue on the next row. The top row has indices 0 through 15; the next row starts at 16; the bottom-right cell is 255.

For a cell at row row and column column, its index is action = row * 16 + column. For example, row 2, column 3 has index 35.

A match contains two games

Each match consists of exactly 2 sequential games with colors and first move swapped.

  • Game 1: player 0 is Blue; player 1 is Orange.
  • Game 2: player 1 is Blue; player 0 is Orange.
  • Both games start from an empty board and use the same rules.
  • The games are played in order: finish and score game 1, then start game 2 on a new empty board.

Reading the viewer

Blue moves first; Orange moves second. Stones have a soft glowing rim. More saturated territory indicates stronger local influence during play. This shading is a visual guide; ownership always follows the distance-layer scoring rules. At the end of each game, all Blue territory uses one fixed blue and all Orange territory one fixed orange.

When a game ends

  • A game ends immediately when no legal placement remains. Neither player receives an extra turn.
  • When game 1 ends, its final score is available to both players throughout game 2. You may adapt your strategy to that score difference.
  • The match ends once both games have ended, unless a player forfeits earlier.

 Territory Scoring

When a game ends, score all 256 cells, including occupied cells and empty cells where placement is forbidden. Each cell is worth at most 1 point.

Distance layers

Measure the straight-line (Euclidean) distance from the cell being scored to each stone. Stones at the same distance form a distance layer.

  • dr is the difference between the row of the cell being scored and the row of a stone.
  • dc is the difference between the column of the cell being scored and the column of that stone.

You can compare squared distances exactly using dr * dr + dc * dc. This gives the same distance order without square roots.

Who receives the point?

  1. Inspect the distance layers from nearest to farthest.
  2. In the current layer, count the Blue stones and the Orange stones.
  3. If one color has more stones, that color receives 1 point for the cell. Stop scoring this cell.
  4. If the counts are equal, ignore that layer and inspect the next one. Do not carry its counts forward.
  5. If every layer is tied, the cell is unclaimed and neither color receives a point.

An occupied cell belongs to its own stone's color, because that stone is at distance 0.

Example: the nearest layer contains 1 Blue stone and 1 Orange stone. Skip that layer. If the next layer contains 2 Blue stones and 1 Orange stone, Blue receives 1 point.

Combined match score

Each player's match score is the sum of their territory points from both games, following their own color on each board. Compare this total; individual game wins do not decide the match.

Example: player 0 scores 130 against 126 in game 1, then 120 against 136 in game 2. The combined scores are 250 against 262, so player 1 wins the match even though each player won one game.

Victory Conditions
  • Finish both games with a higher combined territory score than your opponent.
  • Or, your opponent forfeits the match.
Defeat Conditions
  • Finish both games with a lower combined territory score than your opponent.
  • Or, exceed the response time limit, produce malformed output, or choose an illegal action.

A forfeit ends the entire match, regardless of territory already scored.

Draw Conditions
Finish both games with equal combined territory scores.

Leagues

There are 3 leagues. The rules and input/output protocol are identical in all leagues; only the league boss changes.

  • League 1: a greedy territory-influence baseline.
  • League 2: an intermediate trained neural policy (iteration-003160), choosing its highest-rated legal move without search.
  • League 3: a trained neural policy, choosing its highest-rated legal move without search.

 Game Protocol

Input per game turn

Line 1: five space-separated values, in this order: gameId side ply myScore opponentScore.

They are all integers except for side.

  • gameId: the game on which you must act, 1 or 2.
  • side: your color on this board, a single character, B for Blue or O for Orange.
  • ply: the number of stones already placed on this board.
  • myScore: your combined territory score from completed games only.
  • opponentScore: your opponent's combined territory score from completed games only.

Both score values are 0 in game 1 and contain the final game 1 scores throughout game 2. They do not include territory on the active board.

Next 16 lines: the board rows, from top to bottom. Each row is a string of exactly 16 characters without spaces:

  • B: a Blue stone.
  • O: an Orange stone.
  • .: an empty cell, which may or may not be a legal placement.

Next line: an integer legalActionCount, the number of legal placements available on this board for this turn.

Next legalActionCount lines: one integer action per line, identifying a legal placement using the cell numbering defined in Rules.

Output per game turn
One line: a single integer action from the supplied list of legal actions.
Constraints
  • Each match has 2 players.
  • 1 ≤ gameId ≤ 2.
  • 1 ≤ legalActionCount ≤ 256 whenever input is sent.
  • 0 ≤ action ≤ 255.
  • Response time for your first decision of the match: 1000 milliseconds.
  • Response time for each later decision: 100 milliseconds, including your first decision in game 2.

Starter Bot: One-Ply Greedy (C++17)

To start playing, select C++ in the IDE, replace the editor contents with this complete program, and click Play my code.

The bot tries each supplied legal action, scores the resulting position using the territory rules, and chooses the largest difference between its own and its opponent's territory. Equal evaluations keep the first action in the supplied list.

This is an entry-level baseline. It looks only one move ahead and does not predict the opponent's reply. It is not guaranteed to beat the bosses. Territory during play is only a heuristic; the match is decided by the final combined score.

Each input contains the full board. This example rebuilds the position every turn and uses the supplied side, so it needs no persistent history for either game.

// Hexadeca starter bot: choose the best territory difference after one move. #include <array> #include <iostream> #include <string> #include <vector> using namespace std; constexpr int SIZE = 16; constexpr int MAX_DISTANCE_SQUARED = 2 * (SIZE - 1) * (SIZE - 1); struct Stone { int row, column; char side; }; int territoryDifference(const vector<Stone>& stones, char mySide) { int result = 0; for (int row = 0; row < SIZE; ++row) { for (int column = 0; column < SIZE; ++column) { // Each entry counts only ONE squared-distance layer. array<int, MAX_DISTANCE_SQUARED + 1> balance{}; for (const Stone& stone : stones) { int dr = row - stone.row; int dc = column - stone.column; balance[dr * dr + dc * dc] += (stone.side == mySide ? 1 : -1); } for (int difference : balance) { // Tied layers are skipped; their counts are not carried forward. if (difference == 0) continue; result += (difference > 0 ? 1 : -1); break; } // If every layer is tied, this cell adds no points. } } return result; } int main() { ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr); int gameId, ply, myScore, opponentScore; char side; while (cin >> gameId >> side >> ply >> myScore >> opponentScore) { // The full board is provided every turn, so no saved history is needed. // This also handles the second game and swapped colors automatically. vector<Stone> stones; for (int row = 0; row < SIZE; ++row) { string line; cin >> line; for (int column = 0; column < SIZE; ++column) { if (line[column] == 'B') stones.push_back({row, column, 'B'}); if (line[column] == 'O') stones.push_back({row, column, 'O'}); } } int legalActionCount; cin >> legalActionCount; vector<int> actions(legalActionCount); for (int& action : actions) cin >> action; int bestAction = actions.front(); int bestValue = -SIZE * SIZE - 1; for (int action : actions) { stones.push_back({action / SIZE, action % SIZE, side}); int value = territoryDifference(stones, side); stones.pop_back(); if (value > bestValue) { bestValue = value; bestAction = action; } } cout << bestAction << endl; // endl flushes the decision to the referee. } }

Credits and Referee Source

Original game design and CodinGame contribution by Srot.

Download the Java referee and rules source (without league bosses). The placement and territory rules are implemented in HexadecaRules.java; the two-game match is managed by HexadecaMatch.java and Referee.java.

            y = np.stack((a[:,0]+a[:,1]+a[:,2],
                          a[:,1]-a[:,2]-a[:,3]), axis=1)
            result = y.reshape(2, 2, -1, 8, 8).transpose(2, 3, 0, 4, 1).reshape(-1, 256)
        else:
            result = weights.reshape(weights.shape[0], -1) @ x.reshape(channels, 256)
        result *= scale
        result += offset
        return result.reshape(-1, 16, 16)

    def forward(self, features):
        trunk = self.convolution(features, self.layers[0])
        np.maximum(trunk, 0, out=trunk)
        for block in range(10):
            hidden = self.convolution(trunk, self.layers[1 + block * 2])
            np.maximum(hidden, 0, out=hidden)
            hidden = self.convolution(hidden, self.layers[2 + block * 2])
            trunk += hidden
            np.maximum(trunk, 0, out=trunk)
        policy = self.convolution(trunk, self.layers[-1])
        np.maximum(policy, 0, out=policy)
        return self.linear @ policy.reshape(-1) + self.bias


def encode_features(board, history, side, legal_actions):
    features = np.zeros((16, 16, 16), dtype=np.float32)
    cells = np.asarray(board, dtype=np.int8).reshape(16, 16)
    features[0] = cells == 1
    features[1] = cells == -1
    features[2].reshape(-1)[legal_actions] = 1
    if side == 1:
        features[3].fill(1)
    historical = cells.copy().reshape(-1)
    for offset in range(4):
        if offset < len(history):
            historical[history[-offset - 1]] = 0
        features[4 + offset * 2] = (historical == 1).reshape(16, 16)
        features[5 + offset * 2] = (historical == -1).reshape(16, 16)
    marked = set()
    for action in reversed(history):
        color = board[action]
        if color not in marked:
            features[12 if color == 1 else 13].reshape(-1)[action] = 1
            marked.add(color)
        if len(marked) == 2:
            break
    step = np.float32(2.0 / 15.0)
    coordinates = np.asarray([
        np.float32(-1.0 + np.float32(step * i)) if i < 8
        else np.float32(1.0 - np.float32(step * (15 - i)))
        for i in range(16)
    ], dtype=np.float32)
    features[14] = coordinates[:, None]
    features[15] = coordinates[None, :]
    return features


def main():
    with np.load(io.BytesIO(base64.b64decode(WEIGHTS_B64)), allow_pickle=False) as archive:
        model = PolicyModel({name: archive[name] for name in archive.files})
    histories = {1: [], 2: []}
    known = {1: [0] * 256, 2: [0] * 256}
    while True:
        line = sys.stdin.readline()
        if not line:
            return
        game_id, side, ply, my_score, opponent_score = line.split()
        game_id, ply, my_score, opponent_score = map(int, (game_id, ply, my_score, opponent_score))
        side = 1 if side == "B" else 2
        rows = [sys.stdin.readline().strip() for _ in range(16)]
        board = [1 if c == "B" else -1 if c == "O" else 0 for row in rows for c in row]
        count = int(sys.stdin.readline())
        legal = [int(sys.stdin.readline()) for _ in range(count)]
        history = histories[game_id]

        history.append(action)
        known[game_id] = board
        print(action, flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The Goal

Claim more territory than your opponent across 2 games with colors and first move swapped. The higher combined territory score wins the match.

 Rules

Board and placement

  • Each game starts on an empty 16 by 16 board.
  • Blue plays first. Blue and Orange then alternate, placing 1 stone per turn.
  • A placement must be on an empty cell with no stone in any of its 8 neighboring cells, including diagonals. This applies to stones of either color.
  • Neighbors outside the board are ignored. On an empty board, every cell is legal.
  • Stones never move or disappear. Passing is not allowed.

Cell coordinates and action indices

Rows are numbered from 0 at the top to 15 at the bottom. Columns are numbered from 0 on the left to 15 on the right.

Every cell has an integer action index. Start at 0 in the top-left corner, count from left to right, then continue on the next row. The top row has indices 0 through 15; the next row starts at 16; the bottom-right cell is 255.

For a cell at row row and column column, its index is action = row * 16 + column. For example, row 2, column 3 has index 35.

A match contains two games

Each match consists of exactly 2 sequential games with colors and first move swapped.

  • Game 1: player 0 is Blue; player 1 is Orange.
  • Game 2: player 1 is Blue; player 0 is Orange.
  • Both games start from an empty board and use the same rules.
  • The games are played in order: finish and score game 1, then start game 2 on a new empty board.

Reading the viewer

Blue moves first; Orange moves second. Stones have a soft glowing rim. More saturated territory indicates stronger local influence during play. This shading is a visual guide; ownership always follows the distance-layer scoring rules. At the end of each game, all Blue territory uses one fixed blue and all Orange territory one fixed orange.

When a game ends

  • A game ends immediately when no legal placement remains. Neither player receives an extra turn.
  • When game 1 ends, its final score is available to both players throughout game 2. You may adapt your strategy to that score difference.
  • The match ends once both games have ended, unless a player forfeits earlier.

 Territory Scoring

When a game ends, score all 256 cells, including occupied cells and empty cells where placement is forbidden. Each cell is worth at most 1 point.

Distance layers

Measure the straight-line (Euclidean) distance from the cell being scored to each stone. Stones at the same distance form a distance layer.

  • dr is the difference between the row of the cell being scored and the row of a stone.
  • dc is the difference between the column of the cell being scored and the column of that stone.

You can compare squared distances exactly using dr * dr + dc * dc. This gives the same distance order without square roots.

Who receives the point?

  1. Inspect the distance layers from nearest to farthest.
  2. In the current layer, count the Blue stones and the Orange stones.
  3. If one color has more stones, that color receives 1 point for the cell. Stop scoring this cell.
  4. If the counts are equal, ignore that layer and inspect the next one. Do not carry its counts forward.
  5. If every layer is tied, the cell is unclaimed and neither color receives a point.

An occupied cell belongs to its own stone's color, because that stone is at distance 0.

Example: the nearest layer contains 1 Blue stone and 1 Orange stone. Skip that layer. If the next layer contains 2 Blue stones and 1 Orange stone, Blue receives 1 point.

Combined match score

Each player's match score is the sum of their territory points from both games, following their own color on each board. Compare this total; individual game wins do not decide the match.

Example: player 0 scores 130 against 126 in game 1, then 120 against 136 in game 2. The combined scores are 250 against 262, so player 1 wins the match even though each player won one game.

Victory Conditions
  • Finish both games with a higher combined territory score than your opponent.
  • Or, your opponent forfeits the match.
Defeat Conditions
  • Finish both games with a lower combined territory score than your opponent.
  • Or, exceed the response time limit, produce malformed output, or choose an illegal action.

A forfeit ends the entire match, regardless of territory already scored.

Draw Conditions
Finish both games with equal combined territory scores.

Leagues

There are 3 leagues. The rules and input/output protocol are identical in all leagues; only the league boss changes.

  • League 1: a greedy territory-influence baseline.
  • League 2: an intermediate trained neural policy (iteration-003160), choosing its highest-rated legal move without search.
  • League 3: a trained neural policy, choosing its highest-rated legal move without search.

 Game Protocol

Input per game turn

Line 1: five space-separated values, in this order: gameId side ply myScore opponentScore.

They are all integers except for side.

  • gameId: the game on which you must act, 1 or 2.
  • side: your color on this board, a single character, B for Blue or O for Orange.
  • ply: the number of stones already placed on this board.
  • myScore: your combined territory score from completed games only.
  • opponentScore: your opponent's combined territory score from completed games only.

Both score values are 0 in game 1 and contain the final game 1 scores throughout game 2. They do not include territory on the active board.

Next 16 lines: the board rows, from top to bottom. Each row is a string of exactly 16 characters without spaces:

  • B: a Blue stone.
  • O: an Orange stone.
  • .: an empty cell, which may or may not be a legal placement.

Next line: an integer legalActionCount, the number of legal placements available on this board for this turn.

Next legalActionCount lines: one integer action per line, identifying a legal placement using the cell numbering defined in Rules.

Output per game turn
One line: a single integer action from the supplied list of legal actions.
Constraints
  • Each match has 2 players.
  • 1 ≤ gameId ≤ 2.
  • 1 ≤ legalActionCount ≤ 256 whenever input is sent.
  • 0 ≤ action ≤ 255.
  • Response time for your first decision of the match: 1000 milliseconds.
  • Response time for each later decision: 100 milliseconds, including your first decision in game 2.

Starter Bot: One-Ply Greedy (C++17)

To start playing, select C++ in the IDE, replace the editor contents with this complete program, and click Play my code.

The bot tries each supplied legal action, scores the resulting position using the territory rules, and chooses the largest difference between its own and its opponent's territory. Equal evaluations keep the first action in the supplied list.

This is an entry-level baseline. It looks only one move ahead and does not predict the opponent's reply. It is not guaranteed to beat the bosses. Territory during play is only a heuristic; the match is decided by the final combined score.

Each input contains the full board. This example rebuilds the position every turn and uses the supplied side, so it needs no persistent history for either game.

// Hexadeca starter bot: choose the best territory difference after one move. #include <array> #include <iostream> #include <string> #include <vector> using namespace std; constexpr int SIZE = 16; constexpr int MAX_DISTANCE_SQUARED = 2 * (SIZE - 1) * (SIZE - 1); struct Stone { int row, column; char side; }; int territoryDifference(const vector<Stone>& stones, char mySide) { int result = 0; for (int row = 0; row < SIZE; ++row) { for (int column = 0; column < SIZE; ++column) { // Each entry counts only ONE squared-distance layer. array<int, MAX_DISTANCE_SQUARED + 1> balance{}; for (const Stone& stone : stones) { int dr = row - stone.row; int dc = column - stone.column; balance[dr * dr + dc * dc] += (stone.side == mySide ? 1 : -1); } for (int difference : balance) { // Tied layers are skipped; their counts are not carried forward. if (difference == 0) continue; result += (difference > 0 ? 1 : -1); break; } // If every layer is tied, this cell adds no points. } } return result; } int main() { ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr); int gameId, ply, myScore, opponentScore; char side; while (cin >> gameId >> side >> ply >> myScore >> opponentScore) { // The full board is provided every turn, so no saved history is needed. // This also handles the second game and swapped colors automatically. vector<Stone> stones; for (int row = 0; row < SIZE; ++row) { string line; cin >> line; for (int column = 0; column < SIZE; ++column) { if (line[column] == 'B') stones.push_back({row, column, 'B'}); if (line[column] == 'O') stones.push_back({row, column, 'O'}); } } int legalActionCount; cin >> legalActionCount; vector<int> actions(legalActionCount); for (int& action : actions) cin >> action; int bestAction = actions.front(); int bestValue = -SIZE * SIZE - 1; for (int action : actions) { stones.push_back({action / SIZE, action % SIZE, side}); int value = territoryDifference(stones, side); stones.pop_back(); if (value > bestValue) { bestValue = value; bestAction = action; } } cout << bestAction << endl; // endl flushes the decision to the referee. } }

Credits and Referee Source

Original game design and CodinGame contribution by Srot.

Download the Java referee and rules source (without league bosses). The placement and territory rules are implemented in HexadecaRules.java; the two-game match is managed by HexadecaMatch.java and Referee.java.
